title: Active Directory
summary: Why the directory is the centre of most enterprise intrusions.

sections.p: The identity and authorisation database of a Windows estate: users, computers, groups, policies and trusts. Control of the directory is effectively control of everything that authenticates against it.

A tiered model separates Tier 0 (domain controllers, identity infrastructure), Tier 1 (servers and applications) and Tier 2 (workstations), and forbids credentials from a higher tier being used on a lower one. Tier violations are how a workstation compromise becomes a domain compromise.
Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Backup Operators, Account Operators, the krbtgt account, GPOs linked to many objects, and any service account with an SPN and an old password.

Kerberoasting (service tickets for offline cracking), AS-REP roasting (accounts without pre-authentication), DCSync (replication rights abused to pull hashes), golden and silver tickets (forged Kerberos tickets), GPO abuse to run code estate-wide, and ACL abuse to grant rights quietly.
Group membership changes on privileged groups, account creation outside change control, 4769 bursts with RC4 encryption, DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All by non-DC accounts, and GPO modifications.

If DCSync or a DC compromise is confirmed, every credential in the domain is suspect. krbtgt must be reset twice with a replication cycle between resets, and recovery planning should assume a rebuild of trust rather than a cleanup.

title: Authentication Attacks
summary: Brute force, spraying, stuffing, and abuse of valid credentials.

sections.p: Attacks that obtain or abuse credentials to authenticate as a legitimate identity, rather than exploiting a software vulnerability.
Valid credentials generate no exploit artefacts, survive patching, and grant exactly the access the legitimate user has. It is the cheapest and most reliable route into most enterprises.

Brute force (many passwords, one account), password spraying (one common password, many accounts, staying under lockout thresholds), credential stuffing (username/password pairs stolen elsewhere), and use of credentials bought from infostealer marketplaces.

sections.h: What it looks like in logs
sections.p: Windows: 4625 bursts, then a 4624 from the same source. The sub-status separates password guessing from username enumeration. Linux: repeated 'Failed password' then 'Accepted password'. Cloud: sign-ins from unfamiliar ASNs, impossible travel, repeated MFA prompts.

Identify the source address and account, count the failures precisely, find the first and last suspicious events, determine whether authentication succeeded, then examine everything the account did afterwards - which is where the intrusion actually begins.

Block the source, reset the credential, revoke sessions and tokens (a reset alone leaves an active session working), remove any attacker-registered MFA method, and check for accounts created or promoted while the credential was live.
T1110 Brute Force, T1110.003 Password Spraying, T1078 Valid Accounts, T1621 MFA Request Generation.
Resetting the password but not revoking sessions; missing the backdoor account created during the window; treating an internal user's two failed attempts as an attack.

title: Phishing
summary: Email as the dominant initial access vector.

sections.p: Messages crafted to make a recipient execute a file, click a credential-harvesting link, or perform an action such as changing payment details.
It scales, requires no vulnerability, and targets the one component that cannot be patched. Targeted variants impersonate real partners and reference real business processes.

Look-alike sender domains, authentication failures (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), Received hops through unrelated infrastructure, urgency and deadlines in the body, and attachments that execute: .lnk, .iso, .img, .html, macro-enabled documents, and password-protected archives whose password is in the message.

A gateway cannot inspect an encrypted archive. Supplying the password in the body defeats content scanning while remaining trivially usable by the victim. Treat that combination as hostile until proven otherwise.

Analyse headers first, then the payload, then scope: how many recipients, how many opened, how many extracted, how many executed. The execution count defines the incident; the delivery count defines the campaign.

Purge from all mailboxes, block the sender domain and its supporting infrastructure, isolate endpoints where execution occurred, reset affected credentials, and issue targeted awareness that names the specific lure.
T1566.001 Spearphishing Attachment, T1566.002 Spearphishing Link, T1204.002 User Execution.
Treating the reporting user as the problem. Users who report are the control that worked; reinforce it publicly.

title: Malware
summary: Loaders, implants and how to triage a sample from a report.

sections.p: Loaders and droppers (establish a foothold and fetch more), remote access implants, infostealers, ransomware encryptors, and living-off-the-land tooling that uses legitimate signed binaries instead of custom code.
Hashes for identification, imports for capability, strings for infrastructure and behaviour, entropy and section names for packing, compile timestamp and signature for provenance.
Sandbox execution recording process, file, registry and network behaviour: mutexes created, persistence written, domains resolved, beacon intervals, injection targets.

VirtualAllocEx with WriteProcessMemory and CreateRemoteThread indicates process injection. CryptEncrypt suggests ransomware. InternetOpenUrl indicates download capability. Capability inferred from imports is more reliable than a family name.

File hashes change with every rebuild and are the weakest indicator. Mutex names, URI paths, user-agents, registry value names and behavioural sequences are baked into the tooling and survive recompilation.

sections.h: What to do with the report
sections.p: Convert every artefact into a hunt query and a detection candidate, then sweep the estate. A triage report that produces no detections has produced nothing.
T1027 Obfuscated Files, T1055 Process Injection, T1204 User Execution, T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer.

title: Persistence
summary: How attackers guarantee they can come back.

sections.p: Any mechanism that returns execution to the attacker after a reboot, a logoff or a cleanup attempt.
Access obtained is access that can be lost. Persistence protects the investment, and experienced operators plant several mechanisms of different types expecting the obvious one to be found.

Run and RunOnce registry values, scheduled tasks, services (7045), WMI event filter and consumer pairs, startup folder shortcuts, DLL search-order hijacking, image file execution options, and accounts added to privileged groups.
cron entries and systemd timers, systemd units, rc scripts, shell profile modifications, SUID binaries, and additional SSH authorized_keys entries.

Enumerate by creation time rather than by suspicion. Everything created during the confirmed attack window deserves inspection. Check WMI subscriptions explicitly - they do not appear in ordinary startup locations.
Remove every mechanism in one coordinated action across all hosts, preserve copies first, then verify with a second sweep. Cleaning one host while others still beacon simply invites redeployment.
T1547.001 Registry Run Keys, T1053.005 Scheduled Task, T1543.003 Windows Service, T1546.003 WMI Event Subscription, T1098.004 SSH Authorized Keys.
Finding one mechanism and stopping. Deleting rather than preserving. Missing a scheduled task that re-downloads the payload after the payload itself is removed.

title: Privilege Escalation
summary: Moving from the rights you have to the rights you want.

sections.p: Obtaining higher privileges on a host or in the directory than the compromised identity originally held.
Before escalation, damage is bounded by one user's access. After it, the attacker can read memory, install services, disable defences and move laterally with stolen credentials.

Weak service or directory permissions allowing binary replacement, unquoted service paths, credential theft from LSASS, token impersonation, vulnerable drivers, and simply adding an account to a privileged group when directory write access exists.
sudo misconfiguration, SUID binaries, writable systemd units or cron files, and kernel exploits.

A process whose integrity level rises without a corresponding UAC prompt, service binaries or configurations modified by non-admin accounts, 4672 for accounts that should never receive special privileges, and group membership changes outside change control.

Compare integrity or privilege state before and after on the same code, identify the specific misconfiguration exploited, and establish what the escalated context then did - usually credential access.
Restore the original binary and correct permissions, treat every credential cached on the host as stolen, and audit privileged group membership across the estate.
T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation, T1574.011 Services Registry Permissions Weakness, T1134 Access Token Manipulation, T1078 Valid Accounts.

title: Lateral Movement
summary: Authenticated movement between hosts using stolen credentials.

sections.p: Using credentials obtained on one host to access another, repeated until the attacker reaches the systems they actually want.
Initial access rarely lands on the valuable system. Movement converts a foothold into reach - and because it uses valid credentials, it looks like administration.

Remote service creation (PsExec: 4648, Type 3 logon, ADMIN$ access, 7045 PSEXESVC), WMI remote execution, WinRM, RDP (Type 10), remote scheduled tasks, and pass-the-hash producing NTLM network logons.

Most SMB-based movement produces the same sequence: explicit credentials supplied, a network logon on the destination, administrative share access, and a new service. Recognising that shape lets you count movements quickly.

Build a movement graph: source host, destination host, account, method, timestamp. Count distinct destinations per account per hour - humans, scripts and management tooling have very different shapes.

A destination returning 0xC000015B is refusing the logon type, typically because segmentation or a tiered admin model denies network logon to that account. That is a control working, and it belongs in the report.
Disable the account used for movement, isolate affected hosts simultaneously, and assume credentials cached on every visited host are compromised.
T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares, T1021.001 Remote Desktop, T1569.002 Service Execution, T1047 WMI.

title: Command & Control
summary: The channel between implant and operator.

sections.p: The communication path an implant uses to receive instructions and return results.
C2 is the one stage an attacker cannot skip on a persistent intrusion. Mapping every channel is what makes containment effective; blocking one address rarely ends anything.

HTTP and HTTPS to attacker infrastructure or through a redirector, DNS (queries and TXT answers), legitimate cloud and collaboration services used as dead drops, SMB named pipes for internal pivots, and occasionally ICMP or other protocols.

Fixed intervals with jitter are standard; long-sleep implants that wake hourly or daily exist specifically to survive containment of the primary channel. Average the intervals rather than judging by eye.
TLS client fingerprints (JA3), certificate anomalies (self-signed, CN=localhost, freshly issued), hardcoded user-agents and consistent URI paths identify tooling across rotating infrastructure.

Hosts with no internet route are controlled through a relay - typically an SMB named pipe to a peer that does have egress. If a compromised host cannot reach the internet, find what it is talking to instead.
Block every channel simultaneously: external addresses and domains, DNS sinkholing, and isolation of the relay host. Sequential blocking warns a human operator to adapt.
T1071.001 Web Protocols, T1071.004 DNS, T1090.001 Internal Proxy, T1573 Encrypted Channel, T1102 Web Service.

title: Data Exfiltration
summary: Collection, staging and transfer of stolen data.

sections.p: Collection (finding and reading the data), staging (compressing and often encrypting it into archives, usually in a temp or public directory), and transfer (over C2, DNS, cloud storage, email or removable media).
Each phase leaves different evidence. The staging archive is usually the best single artefact for quantifying impact, because it states exactly what was collected.

The C2 channel itself for bulk data, DNS tunnelling for low-bandwidth or covert movement, commercial cloud storage via tools such as rclone, webmail, and physical media. Cloud storage is favoured because the destination is a legitimate service that most egress policies allow.

Convert what you observe into bytes and compare it against what was staged. DNS tunnels carry very little per query, so a large gap between staged volume and tunnel capacity proves another channel exists.
File counts, data classification, record counts and the specific shares or datasets accessed - and also what was not accessible. Legal and privacy teams need scope, not traffic descriptions.
Archives are commonly deleted after transfer. Volume shadow copies, USN journal entries and prefetch frequently defeat this.
T1074.001 Local Data Staging, T1560.001 Archive via Utility, T1048.003 Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol, T1567.002 Exfiltration to Cloud Storage.

title: Threat Intelligence
summary: Turning knowledge about adversaries into better decisions.

sections.p: Tactical intelligence is indicators - short-lived and immediately actionable. Operational intelligence is tradecraft: tools, techniques and sequencing. Strategic intelligence is targeting, motive and trend.

A confidence judgement, never a certainty. It rests on overlap across multiple independent axes: infrastructure, tooling artefacts, tradecraft and targeting. A single shared IP proves nothing; hosting is shared.
State low, moderate or high confidence, the evidence supporting it, and what would change your assessment. Analysts who never express uncertainty are eventually wrong in public.
Intelligence must change a decision. If the actor's profile says exfiltration precedes extortion within 72 hours, containment urgency changes. If it does not change anything, it is decoration.
The same group carries different names across vendors. Track the behaviour and the artefacts; treat the name as a label for correlation, not as knowledge in itself.
Using intelligence to skip evidence collection, over-attributing on commodity tooling, or letting a compelling actor narrative drive conclusions the logs do not support.
